title: Conduction System and the Electrocardiogram
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the heart generates its own rhythm and carries it through the atria and ventricles in a fixed order. It covers conduction anatomy and blood supply, pacemaker ion currents, and how the electrocardiogram (ECG) records these events, then applies them to blocks, arrhythmias, accessory pathways, and sinus node disease. Board questions usually give a strip, a lead group, or a clinical setting and ask you to work back to the structure, ion current, or artery responsible. If you can explain why the AV node is slow, why the Purkinje system is fast, and which way a wave of depolarization moves relative to a lead, you can reason through most ECG questions.
prerequisites: Resting membrane potential and the Nernst equation for K+, Na+, and Ca2+
Phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential and refractory periods (CV-5)
Gross anatomy of the heart chambers, septa, and fibrous skeleton (CV-2, CV-3)
Coronary artery origins, branches, and dominance (CV-8)
Autonomic receptors and G protein signaling (Gs, Gi, cAMP, protein kinase A)

connections.how: The ventricular action potential that the conduction system triggers is the same one whose plateau and repolarization shape the ST segment and T wave.
Which artery supplies the SA node, AV node, and bundle branches predicts the conduction problems that follow each infarct.
Ischemia slows conduction and alters refractoriness, which creates the substrate for reentrant ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation.
Lyme carditis and maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are classic causes of AV block, linking microbiology and immunology to conduction.
Plasma K+, Ca2+, and Mg2+ set the membrane potential and repolarization of cardiac cells, so electrolyte disorders appear on the ECG.

terms.def: The ability of a cell to depolarize spontaneously to threshold and fire an action potential without an external stimulus.
The slow diastolic depolarization (phase 4) of nodal and Purkinje cells that carries the membrane from its most negative value up to threshold.
An inward current, mainly Na+, carried by HCN channels that open when the membrane hyperpolarizes and that begins phase 4 depolarization.
Suppression of slower latent pacemakers by a faster pacemaker, so the fastest site normally controls the heart.
The property of AV nodal tissue whereby conduction slows progressively as impulses arrive more frequently.
A rhythm generated by a latent pacemaker below the site of failure when the higher pacemaker fails or its impulses are blocked.
The average direction of ventricular depolarization in the frontal plane, expressed in degrees.
The QT interval corrected for heart rate, most often by dividing QT by the square root of the RR interval in seconds (Bazett formula).
Independent activity of atria and ventricles, each driven by its own pacemaker, as in complete heart block.
Repeated reactivation of tissue by an impulse that travels around a circuit, requiring unidirectional block and sufficiently slow conduction.
Extra depolarizations arising during or just after repolarization (early or delayed afterdepolarizations) that can reach threshold.
Early activation of part of the ventricle through an accessory pathway, producing a short PR interval and delta wave.

sections.title: Anatomy of the conduction system and the purpose of AV nodal delay

blocks.text: Cardiac myocytes are joined by gap junctions, so current passes directly from cell to cell. The conduction system imposes order on this syncytium: a fast pacemaker high in the right atrium, a deliberate delay at the only electrical gateway into the ventricles, and a high-speed distribution network inside them.

The sinoatrial (SA) node lies beneath the epicardium of the right atrium at its junction with the superior vena cava, at the upper end of the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis inside). The impulse spreads through atrial muscle, reaching the left atrium through the anterior interatrial band. The atrioventricular (AV) node sits in the lower interatrial septum within the triangle of Koch (coronary sinus opening, septal tricuspid leaflet, tendon of Todaro). The bundle of His leaves it, pierces the fibrous skeleton, and runs along the lower border of the membranous septum. Because the fibrous skeleton is an insulator, the AV node and His bundle are the only normal electrical path from atria to ventricles.

The right bundle branch descends the right side of the septum, partly through the moderator band to the anterior papillary muscle, so that muscle tenses its chordae before the free wall contracts. The left bundle fans into anterior and posterior fascicles. Both end in subendocardial Purkinje fibers, which activate the apex and septum before the base and the wall from endocardium to epicardium.

blocks.name: conduction-pathway
blocks.caption: SA node through the atria to the AV node, bundle of His, right and left bundle branches, and subendocardial Purkinje fibers.

blocks.text: Conduction velocity depends on fiber diameter, gap junction density, and the upstroke current. Purkinje fibers are large, well coupled, and use fast Na+ channels; AV nodal cells are small, poorly coupled, rest near -60 mV, and depolarize through slow L-type Ca2+ channels.

blocks.title: Conduction speed and intrinsic rate along the pathway
rows: About 100 bpm denervated; 60 to 100 at rest (vagal tone)
blocks.caption: Fastest to slowest: Purkinje, atrial muscle, ventricular muscle, AV node. Rate falls with distance from the SA node, setting the escape hierarchy.

blocks.text: The impulse reaches the AV node about 0.03 s after leaving the SA node, is held about 0.09 s in the node and 0.04 s in the penetrating bundle (total AV delay about 0.13 s), then crosses the whole ventricle through the His-Purkinje system in well under 0.1 s, which keeps the QRS narrow. The delay lets atrial systole, which adds up to about 20% of filling at rest and more when the ventricle is stiff or the rate fast, finish before the AV valves close, raising end-diastolic volume and stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism. The node also filters: its refractory period outlasts its action potential, so when the atria fire 300 to 600 times per minute in flutter or fibrillation, most impulses are blocked. An accessory pathway removes both the delay and the filter (C07). When conduction must travel myocyte to myocyte instead, as in bundle branch block or a ventricular ectopic beat, contraction becomes less synchronous.

sections.title: The pacemaker action potential and its autonomic control

blocks.text: Working myocytes rest near -85 to -90 mV because inward rectifier K+ channels (IK1) clamp the membrane near the K+ equilibrium potential. Nodal cells have very few IK1 channels, so after each beat their membrane drifts toward threshold. This instability is the basis of automaticity. Their most negative value, the maximum diastolic potential, is about -60 mV, where most fast Na+ channels are inactivated.

items: Phase 4: HCN channels open on repolarization and carry the funny current (If), mainly Na+ influx; delayed rectifier K+ current is switching off; late in phase 4, T-type Ca2+ current and Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (extruded by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger) add inward current.
Phase 0: at about -40 mV, L-type Ca2+ channels open, giving a slow, small upstroke.
Phase 3: L-type channels inactivate and delayed rectifier K+ efflux returns the cell to about -60 mV.
There is no phase 1 notch or phase 2 plateau. Refractoriness outlasts repolarization because Ca2+ channel recovery is time dependent.

blocks.name: pacemaker-ap
blocks.caption: SA nodal action potential: phase 4 rise from If and T-type Ca2+ current, Ca2+-driven phase 0 at about -40 mV, and phase 3 K+ repolarization to about -60 mV.

blocks.name: ventricular-ap
blocks.caption: Ventricular myocyte action potential for comparison: stable phase 4 near -90 mV, fast Na+ phase 0, phase 1 notch, Ca2+ plateau (phase 2), and K+ repolarization (phase 3).

blocks.text: Rate depends on the phase 4 slope, the maximum diastolic potential, and the threshold. The SA node has the steepest slope, so it fires first and depolarizes latent pacemakers before they reach threshold. Driving them faster than their own rate also loads them with Na+, increasing electrogenic Na+/K+-ATPase activity and hyperpolarizing them (overdrive suppression), which is why a latent pacemaker often pauses before it escapes when the SA node stops.

A denervated SA node fires at about 100 bpm, so a resting rate of 60 to 80 bpm reflects tonic vagal restraint. Sympathetic stimulation acts through beta-1 receptors and Gs, as shown below, raising rate and speeding AV conduction (shorter PR).

blocks.title: Sympathetic acceleration of the SA node
steps: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptors on nodal cells
Gs activates adenylyl cyclase; cAMP rises
cAMP binds HCN channels directly; If increases
Protein kinase A phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels
Phase 4 steepens; threshold is reached sooner
Rate rises; AV conduction speeds
blocks.caption: cAMP shifts HCN activation to less negative voltages, and protein kinase A increases Ca2+ current.

blocks.text: Acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors coupled to Gi. The alpha subunit lowers cAMP, reducing If; the beta-gamma subunits open acetylcholine-activated K+ channels (IKACh), making the maximum diastolic potential more negative, and reduced Ca2+ current raises the effective threshold. The cell starts lower, climbs more slowly, and must climb further. In the AV node the same changes slow conduction and lengthen the PR; strong vagal discharge, as in the baroreceptor reflex or a vasovagal episode, can cause a sinus pause or transient AV block. Channel blockade confirms the physiology: blocking cardiac L-type Ca2+ channels slows sinus rate and AV conduction with little effect on the ventricular Na+ upstroke, and selective If blockade slows the rate without changing contractility.

blocks.predict: If a drug blocked HCN channels completely, would the SA node stop firing?
blocks.explain: No. T-type Ca2+ current, falling delayed rectifier K+ current, and Ca2+ release with Na+/Ca2+ exchange still depolarize the cell, and it still lacks IK1. The slope flattens and rate falls, but automaticity persists.

sections.title: Blood supply of the nodes and conduction defects in inferior infarction

blocks.text: The conduction system is fed by small coronary branches, so the infarct location predicts the rhythm disturbance. The SA nodal artery arises from the proximal right coronary artery (RCA) in about 60% of hearts and the circumflex in about 40%. The AV nodal artery arises from the artery crossing the crux near the origin of the posterior descending artery, so it comes from the RCA in about 80% (right dominance). Below the node, septal perforators of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) supply the anterior two thirds of the septum, including the right bundle and left anterior fascicle. The His bundle has a dual supply (AV nodal artery and first septal perforator), and the broad left posterior fascicle receives LAD septal branches and the posterior descending artery, which is why isolated posterior fascicular block is uncommon.

Inferior MI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) usually follows RCA occlusion and produces nodal bradyarrhythmias: sinus bradycardia, first degree block, Mobitz I, and sometimes complete block with a narrow junctional escape. Ischemia depresses the Ca2+-dependent nodal action potential, ischemic tissue releases adenosine, which acts on A1 receptors to open the same K+ channels as acetylcholine, and stimulation of vagal afferents in the inferoposterior wall triggers reflex bradycardia and hypotension (the Bezold-Jarisch reflex). Because nodal tissue usually survives and part of the cause is reflex and metabolic, the block is usually transient.

blocks.title: From RCA occlusion to nodal block
steps: Thrombus occludes the proximal RCA
SA and AV nodal arteries lose flow
Ischemia depresses Ca2+-dependent nodal conduction
Adenosine release and inferior wall vagal reflex
IKACh hyperpolarizes nodal cells
Bradycardia, AV block, narrow junctional escape
blocks.caption: The block is in the AV node, so the escape pacemaker lies just below it and uses the normal bundle branches.

blocks.text: Anterior MI from LAD occlusion spares the node but necrotizes septal conduction tissue, giving infranodal block that is less likely to recover and signals a large infarct. In a left-dominant heart a circumflex occlusion can also cause AV nodal block, and because the circumflex supplies the SA node in about 40%, a lateral infarct can cause sinus node dysfunction.

blocks.title: Inferior versus anterior infarction
rows: Sinus bradycardia, first degree, Mobitz I
Ischemia, adenosine, vagal reflex; usually transient
blocks.caption: The artery sets the level of block, and the level sets the escape rhythm and prognosis.

blocks.predict: One patient with complete block has a narrow escape at 50 bpm after an inferior MI; another has a wide escape at 30 bpm after an anterior MI. Whose escape is less stable?
blocks.explain: The anterior MI patient. Infranodal block leaves a distal Purkinje or ventricular pacemaker that is slow, conducts myocyte to myocyte, and may fail. Nodal block leaves a faster, more reliable junctional pacemaker that uses the normal bundle branches.

sections.title: Reading a normal ECG: waves, intervals, rate, and axis

blocks.text: The ECG records the summed dipoles of moving depolarization and repolarization fronts. Depolarization toward a lead's positive electrode is upward, away is downward, and perpendicular is small and biphasic; repolarization gives the opposite sign. At 25 mm/s a small box is 0.04 s and a large box 0.20 s; 10 mm equals 1 mV.

Limb leads view the frontal plane: I (0 degrees), II (+60), III (+120), aVF (+90), aVL (-30), aVR (-150); II equals I plus III (Einthoven's law). V1 to V6 view the horizontal plane. Wall groups: septal V1 to V2 and anterior V3 to V4 (LAD), lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6 (circumflex or diagonals), inferior II, III, aVF (usually RCA).

Atrial repolarization is hidden in the QRS, and the AV node and His bundle are too small to register, so their delay appears as the flat PR segment. The septum depolarizes left to right, giving small septal q waves in I, aVL, V5, V6 and a small r in V1; the thick left ventricle then dominates, giving tall lateral R waves and a deep S in V1 (transition V3 or V4). No gradient exists during the plateau, so ST is isoelectric. Shorter epicardial action potentials make repolarization run epicardium to endocardium, so the T wave is upright where the QRS is upright.

blocks.name: ecg-waveform
blocks.caption: One normal beat with the P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, T wave, and QT interval labeled.

blocks.title: Normal waves and intervals
rows: Under 0.12 s; under 2.5 mm in II
PR interval (onset P to onset QRS)
Atrial and AV nodal plus His-Purkinje conduction
0.06 to 0.10 s; 0.12 s or more abnormal
Same direction as QRS; inverted in aVR
blocks.caption: The QT interval approximates the ventricular action potential duration.

blocks.text: Sinus rhythm means a P wave upright in I and II before every QRS, a constant normal PR, and a rate of 60 to 100 bpm. Regular rate is 300 divided by large boxes between R waves (or 1500 divided by small boxes); for irregular rhythms, count QRS complexes in 10 s and multiply by 6. QT shortens as rate rises, so it is corrected (Bazett: QT divided by the square root of RR in seconds); at normal rates QT is under half the RR.

The normal mean QRS axis is about -30 to +90 degrees. If I and aVF are both positive, the axis is normal; if I is positive and aVF negative, a positive lead II means 0 to -30 (normal) and a negative II means left axis deviation; I negative with aVF positive is right axis deviation; both negative is extreme. Left axis deviation suggests left anterior fascicular block or inferior scar; right axis deviation suggests right ventricular hypertrophy, left posterior fascicular block, or a vertical heart.

blocks.title: Rate, intervals, and axis from a strip
blocks.text: R waves are 4 large boxes apart, with an upright P in II before each QRS. PR is 4 small boxes, QRS 2, QT 9. Lead I is positive, aVF and II negative. Rate is 300 divided by 4, or 75 bpm, sinus rhythm; PR 0.16 s and QRS 0.08 s are normal. QT is 0.36 s; RR is 0.80 s, whose square root is about 0.89, so QTc is about 0.40 s. Axis: I positive and aVF negative place it between 0 and -90, and a negative II puts it beyond -30 (left axis deviation), most likely left anterior fascicular block if there is no inferior infarct.

sections.title: AV blocks and bundle branch blocks

blocks.text: Blocks are classified by site, and the two tissues fail differently. AV nodal cells use slow Ca2+ channels with time-dependent recovery, so the node conducts each closely spaced impulse more slowly (decremental conduction) and fails gradually. His-Purkinje cells use fast Na+ channels and conduct at nearly full speed or not at all, so infranodal block appears suddenly and leaves a slow, unreliable escape.

First degree block is a PR over 0.20 s with every P conducted, usually nodal (athletic vagal tone, nodal-slowing drugs, degeneration). In Mobitz I (Wenckebach) the PR lengthens until a P fails to conduct, then resets; the PR increment is largest after the pause, so RR intervals shorten before the drop and beats group. It is usually nodal, narrow, and benign. In Mobitz II the PR of conducted beats is constant and P waves drop suddenly, indicating His or bundle branch disease; the QRS is often wide and progression to complete block is a risk. In 2:1 block the type cannot be judged from the PR; a wide QRS favors an infranodal site. In third degree block P waves and QRS complexes march independently (AV dissociation), with a junctional or ventricular escape depending on the level. Causes include fibrosis, MI, Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi), sarcoidosis, and maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies injuring the fetal AV node.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the AV blocks
rows: Narrow if junctional, wide if ventricular
blocks.caption: Gradual PR change means AV node; all-or-none failure means His-Purkinje tissue.

blocks.text: When a bundle branch fails, its ventricle is activated late by myocyte-to-myocyte spread, the QRS reaches 0.12 s or more, the terminal QRS points toward the late ventricle, and ST-T changes point opposite to it. In RBBB, septal activation from the left bundle is preserved; causes include right ventricular strain (pulmonary embolism, atrial septal defect) and septal infarction, and it can be normal. LBBB reverses septal activation and almost always means structural heart disease (ischemia, hypertension, aortic stenosis, cardiomyopathy); it can mask a new infarct.

blocks.title: Right versus left bundle branch block
rows: Wide slurred S; septal q kept
Broad notched R; no septal q
blocks.caption: Both have a QRS of 0.12 s or more; incomplete block shows the same pattern at about 0.10 to 0.12 s.

blocks.text: Left anterior fascicular block shifts the axis to about -45 degrees or beyond with little QRS widening; left posterior fascicular block gives right axis deviation. With bifascicular block (right bundle plus one fascicle), loss of the last fascicle produces complete infranodal block with a wide escape at about 20 to 40 bpm, enough to cause syncope.

Tachyarrhythmias arise from three mechanisms. Abnormal automaticity is a steep phase 4 outside the SA node (catecholamines, stretch, ischemia, electrolytes). Triggered activity is early afterdepolarizations (EADs) during a prolonged plateau or delayed afterdepolarizations in Ca2+-overloaded cells. Reentry, the commonest cause of sustained tachycardia, needs the conditions in the cycle below. It is sustained only when the circuit exceeds the wavelength (conduction velocity times refractory period); slow conduction (ischemia, scar) and short refractoriness (ischemia, atrial remodeling) shorten the wavelength.

blocks.title: A reentrant circuit
steps: Premature impulse reaches a branch point
One limb is refractory (unidirectional block)
Impulse travels slowly down the other limb
Blocked limb recovers meanwhile
Impulse returns up the recovered limb
It re-enters the first limb and the loop repeats
blocks.caption: Blocking a limb or lengthening refractoriness stops it.

blocks.text: A premature atrial contraction (PAC) is an early, abnormal P with a narrow QRS; it resets the SA node, so the pause is less than compensatory. A premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is an early wide QRS with no P and a discordant T; retrograde AV nodal block spares the sinus rhythm, so the pause is fully compensatory. A PVC on the vulnerable peak of the T wave (R on T) can start VF.

In atrial fibrillation, pulmonary vein triggers and a dilated, fibrotic atrium sustain wavelets at about 350 to 600 per minute; the node conducts only impulses that find it recovered, so the rhythm is irregularly irregular. Atrial kick is lost, and left atrial appendage stasis promotes embolic stroke. Atrial flutter is macroreentry around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus; with 2:1 conduction it gives a regular rate near 150 bpm. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is typical of COPD and low K+ or Mg2+. Paroxysmal SVT starts and stops abruptly and is usually AV nodal reentry, which vagal slowing of the node can terminate.

blocks.title: How a premature atrial beat starts AV nodal reentry
blocks.text: The AV node has a fast pathway with a long refractory period and a slow pathway with a short one. A PAC finds the fast pathway refractory and conducts down the slow pathway, so its PR is long. By the time it reaches the lower junction, the fast pathway has recovered, so the impulse travels up it to the atria while also descending the His bundle. Atria and ventricles activate almost together, so the retrograde P is buried in or just after the narrow QRS, sometimes as a pseudo R prime in V1. The impulse then re-enters the slow pathway, and the circuit runs at 150 to 250 bpm.

Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is three or more consecutive ventricular beats over 100 bpm, usually scar reentry; AV dissociation, capture beats, and fusion beats confirm it. Torsades de pointes occurs with a long QT: inherited loss of IKs (KCNQ1) or IKr (KCNH2, hERG) or gain of SCN5A Na+ current; low K+ (which reduces IKr), Mg2+, or Ca2+; or IKr-blocking drugs such as some macrolides and antipsychotics. Ventricular fibrillation (VF), with no output, is the commonest initial rhythm of sudden cardiac death, usually triggered by ischemia.

blocks.title: From long QT to torsades de pointes
steps: Less repolarizing K+ current or persistent Na+ current
Action potential and QT lengthen
L-type Ca2+ channels recover and reopen
Early afterdepolarizations fire premature beats
Uneven repolarization supports reentry
Torsades, which may degenerate to VF
blocks.caption: A long QTc carries risk even in an asymptomatic patient.

blocks.title: Tachyarrhythmias at a glance
rows: No P, irregularly irregular narrow QRS
3 or more P shapes, irregular, over 100
blocks.caption: Narrow QRS means His-Purkinje activation; wide means ventricular origin or aberrant conduction.

sections.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and sick sinus syndrome

blocks.text: Incomplete separation of atrial and ventricular muscle by the fibrous AV rings leaves an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) of fast Na+-dependent muscle that usually lacks decremental conduction. Preexcitation on the ECG is the Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern; with tachycardia episodes it is WPW syndrome. Ebstein anomaly is an association. Vagal slowing of the node enlarges the delta wave, and sympathetic drive can hide it; concealed pathways conduct only retrogradely and show no delta wave but still support reentry.

blocks.title: How an accessory pathway produces the WPW pattern
steps: Atria depolarize normally
Impulse crosses the pathway without nodal delay
Part of the ventricle activates early: PR under 0.12 s
Slow cell-to-cell spread forms the delta wave
Impulse via the AV node activates the rest rapidly
Wide fusion QRS with secondary ST-T changes
blocks.caption: The pathway bypasses the AV node but enters outside the Purkinje network.

blocks.text: In orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia the impulse descends the node and returns up the pathway, so the QRS is narrow and the delta wave disappears; antidromic tachycardia descends the pathway and gives a wide, fully preexcited QRS. Atrial fibrillation is the danger. The pathway lacks the node's long, time-dependent refractoriness, so with a refractory period near 0.25 s it can pass about 240 impulses per minute or more, giving an irregular, very fast, wide-complex rhythm whose QRS shape varies with fusion. Short diastole and impulses landing in the vulnerable period allow degeneration to VF. Slowing the AV node does not slow this response and can shift more conduction onto the pathway.

Sick sinus syndrome is intrinsic failure of the SA node, usually from degenerative fibrosis in older adults, and less often from SA nodal artery ischemia, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or inherited channel defects. It often coexists with AV conduction disease and atrial fibrillation. Fewer pacemaker cells give inappropriate sinus bradycardia and chronotropic incompetence (poor rate rise with exercise). In sinus arrest the node fails to fire, so the pause is not a multiple of the P to P interval; in SA exit block the impulse forms but cannot leave the node, so the pause is an exact multiple. Physiologic bradycardia from vagal tone and extrinsic causes such as hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia, or nodal-slowing drugs mimic it but resolve when the cause is removed.

In the tachy-brady form, the fibrotic atria produce paroxysms of fibrillation or flutter that overdrive suppress the diseased node. When the tachycardia stops, the node recovers slowly, and the pause of several seconds causes dizziness or syncope; fatigue reflects poor rate response.

blocks.predict: A 78-year-old has paroxysms of atrial fibrillation, each followed by a 5-second pause before a sinus P wave. Why does the pause follow the tachycardia?
blocks.explain: The rapid atrial rhythm overdrive suppresses the SA node. A healthy node recovers within about 1.5 s, but a fibrotic node with few pacemaker cells recovers slowly, so nothing fires until it or an escape pacemaker reaches threshold.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology explain the wiring. The fibrous skeleton that anchors the valves insulates the atria from the ventricles, and incomplete formation of the AV rings leaves accessory pathways. The conduction system is modified cardiac muscle, so it fails through the processes that damage muscle: ischemia, fibrosis, infiltration (sarcoidosis, amyloid), and inflammation, including Lyme carditis and maternal anti-Ro/SSA injury to the fetal AV node. Coronary anatomy decides which part is lost, with the RCA usually feeding the nodes and the LAD the bundle branches.

Physiology and pathology explain the behavior. Each ECG finding traces to a current: If and Ca2+ currents set rate, Ca2+-dependent nodal conduction sets the PR, fast Na+ conduction keeps the QRS narrow, and K+ currents set the QT, so electrolyte disorders from the kidney or gut appear on the ECG and single-gene channelopathies cause sudden death in structurally normal hearts. The ECG shows electrical activity, not contraction, the nodes and His bundle are inferred from timing rather than seen, and reference values vary slightly with source, age, and sex, so borderline values are read with the whole tracing.

summary: The SA node paces the heart because its phase 4 slope is steepest; overdrive suppression holds latent pacemakers in check.
The AV node and His bundle are the only normal link through the insulating fibrous skeleton; AV delay of about 0.13 s lets atrial systole finish filling and the node filters rapid atrial impulses.
Conduction is fastest in Purkinje fibers and slowest in the AV node, reflecting fiber size, gap junctions, and Na+ versus Ca2+ upstrokes.
Nodal cells lack IK1, so If and T-type Ca2+ current depolarize phase 4; sympathetic cAMP steepens it, and vagal IKACh and low cAMP flatten it.
Inferior MI (RCA) causes transient nodal block with a narrow escape; anterior MI (LAD) causes infranodal block with a wide, slow escape and worse prognosis.
Depolarization toward a positive electrode is positive; rate is 300 divided by large boxes, and leads I, aVF, and II place the axis.
Progressive PR lengthening (Mobitz I) means nodal block; constant PR with sudden drops (Mobitz II) means infranodal block with high risk.
RBBB gives rSR prime in V1 with septal q kept; LBBB gives broad notched lateral R waves with septal q lost.
Reentry needs two pathways, unidirectional block, and slow conduction; long QT causes EAD-triggered torsades.
WPW is short PR, delta wave, and wide QRS from an accessory pathway, dangerous in AF; sick sinus syndrome is fibrotic SA node failure with pauses and tachy-brady episodes.

verify: Conduction velocities and intrinsic pacemaker rates differ slightly between Guyton and Hall, Boron and Boulpaep, and review books; values here are stated as approximate.
Percentages for SA nodal artery origin (about 60% RCA) and AV nodal artery origin (about 80% RCA) vary among anatomical series; confirm the figures NABNE expects.
The atrial contribution to ventricular filling is quoted from about 15% to 30% in different sources; this chapter uses up to about 20% at rest (Guyton and Hall).
QTc upper limits (about 0.45 s in men and 0.46 s in women) follow common consensus guidance, but cutoffs of 0.44 s or 0.47 s also appear in texts.
Lower limit of the normal QRS axis is given as -30 degrees here; some sources use 0 degrees, and the upper limit is sometimes given as +100 degrees.
The atrial rate in atrial fibrillation is quoted variously from 300 to 600 per minute; confirm the range NABNE uses.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Koch triangle, tendon of Todaro, bundle of Kent, and Bezold-Jarisch reflex, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: av-block-strips (first degree, Mobitz I, Mobitz II, and third degree rhythm strips side by side) and bbb-v1-v6 (QRS shapes in V1 and V6 for RBBB and LBBB).
Normal sinus node recovery time after a tachycardia (about 1.5 s or less) is quoted from electrophysiology references; confirm the value NABNE expects if it is tested.
